Resting metabolic rate in the Antillean ghost-faced bat has been quantified through respirometry trials conducted under carefully controlled thermal conditions. At a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate reaches approximately 8.29 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 8.29 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that provides insight into the energetic demands of this small, insectivorous mormoopid. The reproductive output of this species is comparatively low, with females producing a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and typically raising just one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], a pattern that aligns with the slow life-history pace observed in many tropical bat species under the same thermal conditions.

Parturition results in the emergence of a neonate weighing about 3 grams [Wwb = about 3 grams], which represents a substantial maternal investment given the adult female body size. The ultimate wet weight for adult females reaches approximately 11 grams [Wwi = approximately 11 grams], with individuals ranging between 6 and 11 grams depending on age and nutritional status. This modest adult mass places the species among the smaller members of the family Mormoopidae. The rapid postnatal growth phase that follows is energetically demanding, and the pup remains entirely dependent on maternal milk during the earliest weeks of life.

Gestation in Mormoops blainvillei lasts for a period of 85 days [tg = 85 days] at the standard body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a duration that is broadly consistent with that reported for its congener Mormoops megalophylla and reflects the protracted embryogenesis typical of small bats. Under these same thermal conditions, the time from birth to weaning is estimated at 45.5 days [tx = 45.5 days], which allows the pup to achieve nutritional independence before the onset of the energetically costly juvenile phase at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C].

Sexual maturation in this species is a relatively delayed process. Puberty is attained at approximately 365 days after birth [tp = approximately 365 days after birth], and this milestone is observed at a body temperature of 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C], a slightly elevated thermal state likely associated with the heightened metabolic activity of reproductive development. The extended prereproductive period is notable for a bat of this body size and may be linked to the challenges of foraging success and roost fidelity in the Caribbean island environments where the species is endemic.

Maximum recorded longevity for the Antillean ghost-faced bat in natural populations is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], a figure derived from observations on the closely related Mormoops megalophylla and measured at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This remarkably long lifespan relative to body mass positions the species as an extreme example of mammalian slow-life-history evolution. The combination of a single annual reproductive event, a long gestation, an extended juvenile period, and extreme longevity underscores the life-history strategy of a species that prioritizes survival and iteroparity over rapid turnover.
